minor: The (quote) shot narrates only 'Egypt's president put it this way in March 2021.' The Sisi wording, and the fact that it was said at the Suez Canal on 30 March 2021, must be on screen or read aloud. Otherwise the shot has no content.
'Weeks after Egypt's revolution' is about seven weeks (Mubarak resigned 11 Feb 2011; the foundation stone was laid 2 April 2011). This is acceptable but loose.
'Fourteen years' of construction runs from April 2011 to September 2025, about 14.5 years. This is fine as rounded.
'For almost fifty years' covers 1964 to 2011, which is 47 years. This is fine as rounded.
'Drafts already exist' (binding-deal scenario) has no listed source. It most likely refers to the February 2020 Washington draft that Egypt initialed, so say so aloud or add a source.
The 1929 line says the notes 'covered Sudan and British East Africa'. This is correct, but the sources entry only supports the no-upstream-works clause, so add the territorial scope to it.
The UN Security Council 'sent it back to talks led by the African Union'. The presidential statement 'encouraged' AU-led talks, so 'encouraged' would be closer to the source.

shots.vo: This lake on Ethiopia's Blue Nile can hold 74 billion cubic metres of water.
shots.title: *74 billion* m³

shots.vo: It fills behind Africa's largest hydroelectric dam, close to the border with Sudan.
Ethiopia opened it in September 2025, after fourteen years of building.

headline.text: Ethiopia opens Africa's biggest hydropower dam on the Blue Nile

shots.title: September *2025*

shots.vo: Downstream, Egypt says the Nile gives it about 97 percent of its water.

stat.label: Egypt's water from the Nile, Egyptian government, 2021

shots.title: *97%* of its water

shots.vo: Egypt already imports more wheat than almost anyone; less river could mean importing more.
So why do Egypt and Ethiopia still have no deal on running it?
The answer starts with a treaty signed in 1902.
shots.prompt: duotone archival plate, dark slate and one muted orange: treaty papers with wax seals and a pen on a wooden desk in a 1902 palace room, figures in the background out of focus, no readable text, no signs or lettering on any storefront, screen or package
shots.title: Treaty of *1902*

shots.vo: The Nile runs about 6,650 kilometres to the Mediterranean, through a basin shared by eleven countries.
It has two main branches. The White Nile flows out of Lake Victoria; the Blue Nile drops out of Lake Tana in Ethiopia's highlands.
They meet at Khartoum, Sudan's capital. From there, a single river runs north through the Sahara to Egypt.
The branches are not equal: by common estimates the Blue Nile brings about 59 percent of the water reaching Aswan.

chart.title: Ethiopia sends most
chart.source: Sutcliffe and Parks, 1999; Nile Basin Initiative, 2012

shots.vo: Add the Atbara and Sobat, also from Ethiopia, and roughly 85 percent of the Nile starts in its highlands.
Most of it falls between June and September, in one heavy rainy season, then rushes downstream.
On the Blue Nile, close to the Sudan border, stands the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, known as GERD.
Its main wall is 145 metres high and about 1.8 kilometres long.
Behind it, the reservoir can hold 74 billion cubic metres, close to the Nile's whole average yearly flow at Aswan, about 84 billion.

map.label: 74 bn m³ vs 84 bn m³ yearly flow

shots.vo: Its turbines are rated at 5,150 megawatts, more than twice the 2,100 of Egypt's Aswan High Dam.

chart.title: Twice Aswan's power
chart.source: Ethiopian Electric Power, 2025; Egyptian Electricity Holding Company

shots.vo: Ethiopia has more than 120 million people. In 2022, the World Bank estimated, about 45 percent of them still had no electricity.
About 100 kilometres downstream, in a straight line, sits Sudan's Roseires Dam. Whatever GERD releases reaches it first.
In July 2020, Sudan's irrigation ministry reported a sudden drop in the river and linked it to GERD's first filling.

headline.text: Sudan reports sudden fall in Blue Nile, points to Ethiopian dam

shots.vo: Sudanese officials have also said the dam can steady the river and cut floods. For Sudan, it cuts both ways.
To the north-west, along the same border, lies al-Fashaga, farmland claimed by both Sudan and Ethiopia, where troops have clashed since late 2020.
Far to the north, the river fills Lake Nasser behind the Aswan High Dam, finished in 1970.
Lake Nasser can hold about 162 billion cubic metres, Egypt's reserve against bad years.
Below it, Egypt's more than 105 million people live mostly along a narrow green strip of river and delta.
One country holds the tap; another holds most of the people downstream. The rules between them were written, mostly, by others.
In 1902, Britain occupied Egypt and ran Sudan jointly with it. Ethiopia, under Emperor Menelik II, was independent.
That May, Menelik signed a treaty with Britain fixing much of the Ethiopia–Sudan border.
Its Article III says he will not build works on the Blue Nile, Lake Tana or the Sobat that would arrest their flow, without British and Sudanese agreement.

document.title: Treaty between the United Kingdom and Ethiopia, Addis Ababa, 15 May 1902
document.highlight: ...not to construct, or allow to be constructed, any work across the Blue Nile, Lake Tana, or the Sobat which would arrest the flow of their waters into the Nile...

shots.vo: Egypt calls the clause valid; Ethiopia says it was never ratified. The 1902 border is drawn, Lake Tana and the Blue Nile shaded restricted.
In 1929, an exchange of notes between Britain and Egypt went further: no works upstream that would cut Egypt's water or change its timing.

document.title: Exchange of Notes between the United Kingdom and Egypt on the Waters of the Nile, 7 May 1929
document.highlight: Save with the previous agreement of the Egyptian Government, no irrigation or power works... which would... reduce the quantity of water arriving in Egypt, or modify the date of its arrival...

shots.vo: It covered Sudan and British East Africa. Ethiopia was outside it; Egypt reads it as a veto.
After independence, Egypt planned a giant dam at Aswan. In 1959 it signed a new water deal with newly independent Sudan.
Of an average 84 billion cubic metres a year, Egypt got 55.5 and Sudan 18.5; about 10 were set aside for evaporation.
Ethiopia, where most of that water rises, received nothing and was not at the table. On the map, Egypt and Sudan are shaded and Ethiopia is left blank.
The High Dam ended the Nile's yearly flood in Egypt, storing water through the dry years that followed.
Upstream, a US Bureau of Reclamation survey published in 1964 mapped Blue Nile dam sites for Ethiopia, including one near the Sudan border.
For almost fifty years, no large dam was built on the main Blue Nile in Ethiopia: the 1964 survey sites stay empty on the map until the GERD marker appears in 2011.
In May 2010, upstream states signed a Cooperative Framework Agreement in Entebbe, built on 'equitable and reasonable' use, not fixed shares.
Egypt and Sudan refused it. After South Sudan ratified, it entered into force in October 2024, with six members.

map.label: In force Oct 2024 | Egypt, Sudan: outside

shots.vo: In April 2011, weeks after Egypt's revolution, Ethiopia laid the foundation stone of GERD.

clip.tags: working site, excavator, construction, site, equipment, digger, machine, develop, industrial, construction site, construction equipment, dig, bulldozer, under construction, development, teamwork, aerial view

shots.vo: Ethiopia paid largely by itself, from its budget, bonds and public contributions. The reported cost: about five billion dollars.
In March 2015, the leaders of Egypt, Sudan and Ethiopia signed a Declaration of Principles in Khartoum, pledging to avoid 'significant harm'.

document.title: Agreement on Declaration of Principles on the GERD, Khartoum, 23 March 2015
document.highlight: The Three Countries shall take all appropriate measures to prevent the causing of significant harm in utilizing the Blue/Main Nile.

shots.vo: It set no numbers: not how fast to fill, nor how much to release in a drought. That line was never drawn.
Talks under the US Treasury and the World Bank ended in February 2020: Egypt initialed a draft, Ethiopia stayed away.

headline.text: Ethiopia says first filling of Nile dam done; Egypt and Sudan object

shots.vo: Ethiopia announced the first filling in July 2020, saying the rains had done it. Egypt and Sudan objected.
Filling went on each rainy season. By September 2024, Ethiopia had announced the fifth stage.
The first turbine began generating in February 2022; the dam was formally opened in September 2025.
In October 2020, US President Donald Trump said Egypt could end up 'blowing up' the dam. Ethiopia summoned the US ambassador in protest.

headline.text: Trump says Egypt could end up 'blowing up' Nile dam; Ethiopia protests

shots.vo: The UN Security Council met on the dam in 2020 and 2021, then sent it back to talks led by the African Union.

document.title: UN Security Council Presidential Statement S/PRST/2021/18, 15 September 2021
document.highlight: The Security Council encourages Egypt, Ethiopia and Sudan to resume negotiations at the invitation of the Chairperson of the African Union.

shots.vo: The last formal round ended in December 2023. Egypt's water ministry said the talks had failed; Ethiopia blamed Egypt's positions.
Egypt's case starts with scarcity. The UN's FAO puts its renewable water near 550 cubic metres per person a year; below 1,000 counts as scarcity.

chart.title: Egypt below the line
chart.source: FAO AQUASTAT, Egypt profile, 2020; Falkenmark indicator

shots.vo: In a long drought, Egypt argues, a reservoir upstream could hold back water it cannot get anywhere else.
So it wants a binding deal: minimum releases in dry years, and a set way to settle disputes.
Egypt's president put it this way in March 2021.

quote.text: No one can take a drop of water from Egypt, and if it happens there will be inconceivable instability in the region.
quote.who: Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, President of Egypt
quote.source: Remarks at the Suez Canal, 30 March 2021 (Reuters translation)

shots.vo: Ethiopia's case: most of the Nile's water rises on its land, yet old agreements gave it no share.
It says the dam makes electricity, not irrigation, so the water that turns its turbines still flows on downstream.
It will accept guidelines, but not a binding deal it says would lock in the 1959 shares.
And it already sells power across borders, with lines to Sudan, Djibouti and Kenya.
When floods hit Sudan and Egypt's Nile banks in October 2025, Egypt's water ministry blamed the dam's releases.

clip.tags: high water, flood, river, flooding, europe

shots.vo: Ethiopia rejected that, saying the dam had held water back and reduced the floods. Each government cites its own data.
The dispute now reaches the Horn of Africa. In 2024, Ethiopia signed a port deal with Somaliland, and Egypt a defence pact with Somalia.
The dam is finished. What nobody has agreed is what happens in the first long drought.
The Nile has failed before. From 1979 to 1987, its flow ran well below average for nine years.
By 1988, Lake Nasser had fallen close to the lowest level at which Aswan could still make power.
First scenario: a binding deal. Drafts already exist; the open questions are how much GERD releases in drought, and who settles disputes.
On the map, that means agreed minimum flows across the Sudan border every year, and Lake Nasser levels Egypt can plan around.
Second: a long drought with no deal. Both reservoirs could be drawn down at once, and refilling GERD might compete with refilling Lake Nasser.
Then the argument would stop being about treaties. It would be about cubic metres in one year, measured at Roseires and at Aswan.
Third: the new basin commission. With the 2010 framework in force, upstream states can plan their own water projects under its rules.
Egypt and Sudan stay outside it. The basin could split into two legal blocs, upstream and downstream, on one river.
Egypt says it reserves the right to protect its water security.

headline.text: Egypt says dam talks failed, reserves right to protect its water

shots.vo: Ethiopia says it has no intention of harming its neighbours. Which path the river takes may depend as much on the rain as on the talks.
The dam took fourteen years to build. The rules for sharing its river have taken more than a century, and are still unwritten.
Next: the Mekong, where dams upstream in China and Laos shape a river some 60 million people downstream depend on.
